utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. May I ask the Registrar to call the case number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-13a, the Prosecutor versus Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Grant Niemann, I appear together with Mr. Williamson, Mr. Waespi, Ms. Sutherland and Mr. Vos for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am Toma Fila and I am the Defence counsel of Slavko Dokmanovic together with Mr. Petrovic and Ms. Lopicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the accused hear me well in a language accessible to him? Yes. Thank you. All right. We will now proceed with the witness to be called by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Your Honour, this is a witness who has requested full protective measures so he will be testifying with a pseudonym, Witness N as in November. We will also be using the image and voice alteration so after the witness comes in I will have him confirm his name, provide that both to the court and to the Defence and then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask the Prosecutor whether this is the witness whose number is 4 on the list attached to the confidential document filed on 29th January?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, it is. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Number 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. May I ask you to make the solemn declaration, please? WITNESS N (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You may be seated, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time I would like the witness to view this piece of paper and to indicate without saying the name, if this is, in fact, your name. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like to tender this as Prosecutor's Exhibit 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That would be submitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objection from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Examined by MR. WILLIAMSON

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will be referring to you as, "Witness N", during the course of this testimony. So, Witness N, do you recall in July of 1995 speaking with an investigator from the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time did you give a written statement to this investigator and sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time I would like for you to view an item which I will mark as Prosecutor's Exhibit 17, and tell me if you recognise your signature on this document. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is, in fact, your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Okay. At this time, your Honour, I would like to tender this as Prosecutor's Exhibit 17, and I would also tender as Prosecutor's Exhibit 17A a Croatian translation of the same document. Both of these are submitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection? Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Sir, you are originally from Vukovar, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you grow up there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was also born in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you educated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in what field did you receive training initially?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first I studied at secondary engineering school and since I did not manage to get a job in Vukovar I continued my education. I trained as a professional driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point in time were you obligated to do national service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you serve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kraljevo prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you indicated that you had gone back to school. Was this before or after your JNA service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I did my service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you took a job at Vukovar hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In May, only for a certain period of time, but then, on 28th June I got it as a permanent job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, I am sorry, what year was that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the nature of your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was an ambulance driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the circumstances under which you were able to get this job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a job vacancy. I came to replace someone and that is how I stayed on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the situation in Vukovar when you initially took this job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very tense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the reason for this tension?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at that time the shelling of the neighbouring villages had started. Also some parts of town and all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that there was some shelling of neighbouring villages. Was there a point in time when the city of Vukovar began being shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not yet, but later towards the end of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when your family left Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My parents left Vukovar in August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did they leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My daddy is a heart patient so he could not have taken it anyway, and I drove them to Vinkovci and I went back then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your family is Croatian; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were Serbs leaving the town as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you living during the battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When my parents left town I spent a few days at home and then I moved to the hospital permanently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were you accommodated at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few of us found a place where we could stay and where we would not prevent the medical staff from doing their job and we would not bother the patients either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were conditions like at the hospital during this time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first it was not that bad, but then more and more wounded people came into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were your duties as the battle was ongoing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My duties during the battle were to collect the wounded regardless of whether they belonged to the military or whether they were civilians. The important thing was to get them to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so in carrying out these duties were you able to move about freely in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever leave the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you able to pick up the wounded without leaving the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, I did not leave the hospital of my own free will. If there was a call, an emergency call then I would leave the hospital with an ambulance, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you were going out in this ambulance were you able to observe what had happened to the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Every day the city was destroyed more and more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of September did there come a time when you left Vukovar and went to Zagreb for a short period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I drove the wounded to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it difficult for you to get out of the city or to return to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very difficult for me because in the village of Seric there had been a lot of shelling and I almost got killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it necessary for you to pass through the front-lines to go in and out of Vukovar at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the city surrounded entirely or practically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The city was surrounded. There was just this one road across the fields. In order to get to Vinkovci you have to drive through maize fields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this Vukovar's only connection with the outside world at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Vukovar, Bogdanovic, Zidzaric, Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you returned from Zagreb to Vukovar, did you make any other trips outside the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would go out to town, but I did not go out of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it possible to travel outside of Vukovar, after that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was completely surrounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the battle was coming to an end in mid-November, did you become aware of more townspeople gathering at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of why they were coming there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they thought that their only salvation was the hospital because they heard that the international community would be coming in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the JNA's arrival at the hospital after the battle ended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did this occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 18th November 1991 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was happening at the hospital during the course of that evening and into the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That evening some people were being taken away slowly, and the next day they separated us. They separated the men from the women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the morning of 20th are you aware of a meeting which took place inside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not attend the meeting because Dr.Ivankovic said that drivers were not medical staff and he asked us all to go out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you went outside what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of the surgical emergency ward they were separating the men from the women, and we had to stand in a row in a queue all the way to the other side of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that they were separating men from women. Did you see other patients out there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were amongst us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the medical staff was there as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were in the plaster room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you personally after you were made to stand in this line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then soldiers came and they started searching us. After that, on Gunduliceva Street there were five buses and then we all started boarding those buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you start boarding the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who gave you these orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military officers. I do not know what rank he had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this an officer in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got on the bus, who else was on there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My colleagues, drivers, also some of the lightly wounded people and other people who had technical jobs at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also see patients on the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some people I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you after you got on the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I got onto the bus a few minutes later a JNA officer walked in. I do not know what rank he had, whether he was a major, a captain, I could not really tell. He showed us a card that we had, and where it said who was what in the hospital. At that point I did not know what to do, but sitting behind me was Zdravko Dapic, the head of drivers, he was my boss, and when he lifted his card I also raised my card and at that point the officer said that we should go out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other people getting off the bus, buses, under the same circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Out of all five buses only five of us got off, but as far as I know an officer walked into the first two buses only. In the remaining three buses most of the people who were on these remaining buses were technical staff from the hospital who had those cards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after you got off the bus what happened to you? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that same side we stood by the fence, the hospital fence. A few minutes later all the buses turned around and started moving towards the centre. I thought that my colleagues were going to be exchanged and that I had to stay behind and at that point Major Sljivancanin came with a list and he was checking whether we were on that list, and then he asked me what I did at the hospital and after a few moments he sent us back to the hospital again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain at the hospital after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps an hour or two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you during this time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of the emergency surgery ward in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the circumstances under which you were able to leave the hospital eventually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came back, when I stood in front of the emergency ward once again, a soldier took me aside and asked me where I was from. I said that I was from Vukovar. He asked me where, exactly, and I said the name of my street was Narodnih Mucenika and then he asked me where this was and I said that it was at Mitnica and he told me that I should come with him. At that point a lady, Mr. s Vukar, who was a lab technician in the hospital, walked up to him, told him something and at that point he gave me my card back. I hugged her and she accompanied me to the buses that were standing at the other side of the hospital that were waiting for civilians. They were to transport civilians, these buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This woman that got your card back, was she a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And she had worked at the hospital throughout the battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And she intervened on your behalf at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you got on the buses on the other side of the hospital, where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I boarded the bus my boss Zdravko Dapic and I were squatting between the seats on the bus and women covered us up with their coats and bags because the soldiers from the outside were asking for the men to be taken off the buses again. They were shouting, they were banging on the buses. After some time the buses set off towards the centre of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go from there after the buses went into the centre of town? Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They went through the centre of town, then by Velepromet, and then towards Modateks and from Modateks they moved to Negoslavci. From Negoslavci to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to you after your arrival in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived in Sremska Mitrovica we spent the night there. The next day there was an exchange in Bosan Skidvorove.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila? (9.45 am) Cross-examined by MR. FILA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, sir, with your permission I will ask you several questions relating to your testimony. First of all, can you tell us on what day was this that you were just talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, the events at the hospital on 19th and 20th November.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that the military entered on 18th in the afternoon, and on 20th the evacuation of the wounded and the civilians started.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Apologies, your Honours. This is because on page 3, actually page 2 of your statement, a confusion may have been created because the -- it says that the military entered on the 18th and then it says, "the next day", whereas it was really two days later on the 20th so that is what we are trying to point out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he has a question I would suggest that he ask a question and – (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify the dates, that is all, so that I could pose my question. But let us move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was on the 18th in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Marko Mandic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tomica Hegedus and something Lukenda. That was the investigator Lukenda.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You only mentioned the last time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was also on the 18th in the evening. If I remember correctly you said that they were still reported missing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only Glavasevic, not Selemor. He was found in the Ovcara mass grave and the other three, their whereabouts are still unknown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just not to have any misunderstanding, the person called Glavasevic was led away on the 18th and was identified in the Ovcara mass grave. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That same evening I assume that Marko Vlaho was also led away, who was returned two days later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am just reading your statement. You said that Marko had a son, Miroslav, who was led away and it is still -- his whereabouts are still unknown. When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was also on the buses for evacuation in one of the five buses from which I came out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was also the 20th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The buses where you were on the 20th stopped for a while in front of Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Around what time was this? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot. I do not know. I do not know the hour, but it could have been 2 o'clock or 2.30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the afternoon, you mean, not 2 or 3 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I showed you a tape could you perhaps recognise somebody from the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. May we do that? With the court's permission I would like to replay one minute of the Prosecution exhibit number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour. I believe it is a Defence exhibit though, your Honour. I think it is marked Defence Exhibit 2, but no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: While this is being prepared, I only have one additional question. You mentioned a JNA officer came into some of these five buses and when you showed him your ID card he brought you out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is; during all this time have you seen the paramilitary, specifically somebody from Vukovar? Was somebody of these people with them? During all these events in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean was there anybody from the paramilitary there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We do not understand each other well. Besides Major Sljivancanin, this other military, did you see any locals from Vukovar who were not part of the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did see the paramilitary but I think they were not from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you mentioned a son of Dr.Ivankovic, if I believe correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was probably a volunteer. He was wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he wearing a paramilitary or a JNA uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Paramilitary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, you did see somebody from the paramilitary, after all. Were there any others like drivers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would just like you to watch the portion of the videotape, so your Honours, if we could play the videotape, please. (Video played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One single question; have you recognised anybody from the buses in which you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not recognise anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these -- was this personnel from your hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do not know anything. Are you sure that these are not the persons from your hospital because yesterday you did recognise them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not recognise anyone on this bus. On these buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have no additional questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there therefore any objection to the witness being released? No objection? Well, Witness N, thank you so much for coming. You may now be released. (The witness withdrew) (10.00 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, are you going to call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in relation to the next witness, Witness E has previously had protective measures in relation to him and he seeks that the protective measures in relation to him be that he is referred to as Witness E, and that his face be distorted during the course of his testimony. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, could you help with one matter. Velepromet is mentioned in the evidence. We just wanted to know what it is or where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes your Honours. The next witness may be able to help us with that by pointing to it on a photograph and I will get him to give some descriptions of where it is, but briefly, your Honour, it is in the town of Vukovar. It is near the JNA barracks, and it is a being of sorts, like a hangar, I believe, or a storage shed of sorts, but I will ask the witness to expand. This witness should be able to assist us with that, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This next witness who is coming, your Honour, appears as witness number 5 on your Honour's list. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning Witness E, could you please make the solemn declaration. WITNESS E (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Prosecutor? Examined by MR. NIEMANN

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, during the course of your testimony this morning we will refer you to as, "Witness E". Do you understand that? When you answer me, if you could speak the answer, because if you shake your head it cannot be taken down on the transcript, so if you could answer me when I ask you a question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to look at a piece of paper that I am now going to show you, and if the piece of paper contains your name could you say, "yes", or, "no"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might that be shown to the Defence, and your Honours, I tender that under seal as the next Prosecution exhibit in order.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I ask Mr. Fila whether he objects to this document being exhibited, the name --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness E, in -- on 19th June 1995 were you visited by some investigators from the -- from this Tribunal, the International Criminal Tribunal, and during the time of that visit did they obtain from you a statement of the evidence and events that occurred to you in Vukovar during the latter part of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that statement taken in the English language but translated to you in Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the statement had been taken down fully and complete, was it read over to you by an interpreter who read to you the contents of the document and did you agree that it was a true and accurate record of your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the conclusion of events were you then asked to affix your signature to this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you look at the document that I now show you, please? (Handed). There is a Croatian translation of the document, your Honours. Witness E, would you look at the document that appears in the English language and tell me if you see there your signature on each page of that document at the foot of the page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, I tender that statement together with the Croatian translation of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 19 and the Croatian translation, 19A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection from Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness E, were you located in the Vukovar area when the tensions began to escalate in the latter part of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you involved in -- at that time -- were you yourself involved in civil protection which included providing food and medical supplies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you then later involved in that activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you might explain to us what you were doing and at what time this was, in terms of months and days, if possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this was in May of 1991 when the policemen were killed in Borovo Selo. In my opinion that is when the trouble started in the territory of the city of Vukovar. Up until then we had believed that such things would not happen. However, after the murder of the Croatian policemen we saw that something was being prepared, that something was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what did you see was being prepared and what did you think was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the indicators was the departure of people of Serbian ethnic origin from Vukovar. First they took a raft across to the Republic of Serbia and people were leaving en mass. Our friends of the Serbian ethnic origins were leaving. They were asking them why, where were they going and why. They did not want to say why. But they were saying that they were threatened in the Republic of Croatia. That is in the city of Vukovar. I asked several of my friends who were leaving the city, "please tell me, why are you leaving?" They would shrug their shoulders and they would say, "we believe you will see it soon too". The others who did not leave by this ferry or whatever means, would go to the barracks and the military transported them in their vehicles towards Borovo Selo. Since I live on the main street in Vukovar, every day you could see the departure of these people. Of course, this was an indication, and it was obvious to us that something would happen, that is that something was being prepared, but even then we could not comprehend what was to follow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the ferry or raft you spoke about a moment ago, that was crossing the Danube River to the Republic of Serbia on the other side. Is that right? (10.15 am)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the military barracks where these people were also being gathered and taken from by military transport was the JNA barracks in Vukovar. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The only barracks in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during the time of the siege of Vukovar, were conditions for the people of Vukovar very difficult?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were very difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there shortages of food and electricity and the essentials of life during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first shelling of Vukovar was -- took place some time in July of 1991. The shells started falling in the city without any prior warning or any kind of notice. They started falling suddenly. Naturally, panic ensued in the city and everybody had to fend for themselves so that they would save themselves and the lives of their own, and the lives of people who could not take care of themselves, naturally. After a while, Vukovar was blocked. That means it was surrounded by all four cardinal directions and remained surrounded for three months. In the city itself there was no electricity, no water. The food supplies that were there would spoil fast, so that people were having difficulties in their attempt to survive during the siege of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in order to protect yourselves and fellow citizens of Vukovar from the constant shelling, did you take shelter in an establishment near the hospital of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The location of Vukovar is such that it had some natural protection, and some that were man-made, namely nuclear shelter and also some cellars and basements in big apartment buildings. I was in one of these buildings across the street from the Vukovar hospital. This was a store of the enterprise Vupic from Vukovar. In this shelter underneath the store there were about 60 persons. They were of different ethnic origins. There were ethnic Serbs and ethnic Croats. I think it was about 50/50, the ratio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long were you in this cellar of the Vupic building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were there about two and a half months until the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you were in this shelter did you from time to time receive reports from people who were coming and going as to the events that were happening outside in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you subsequently come to learn of the fact that there were negotiations going on in order to achieve a peaceful evacuation of the citizens of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you find out about this, and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since the shelter that I was in, together with the other citizens, was right next door to the hospital in Vukovar which was the major target of shelling, taking into account all the facilities in Vukovar, and in the immediate vicinity of the hospital was the building of the Ministry of the Interior in Vukovar, so all of this was within a diameter of 100 metres, and of course we were wondering what would happen. I found out that negotiations were underway with the then Yugoslav People's Army on the surrender of the town of Vukovar, so that people, civilians -- and I estimate their number to be 10-12,000 in the town itself and there were a lot of people who were wounded too, that is to say so that people could leave of their own free will, go wherever they wanted to go, and that in return the city would surrender to the then Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know when this was to occur? When did you understand that would happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my opinion, in my opinion, this was supposed to take place very early. So that the killing of people and destruction of property would be avoided. However, these negotiations seemed to be very painstaking, very difficult and very long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you learn that an agreement was finally reached in relation to the evacuation of the citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since the building of the Ministry of the Interior was set on fire, the employees together with the then director moved into our shelter together with us because it was rather big and there was enough room. Mr. Polak, Stjepan, who was director then, he was the head of police in the town of Vukovar, he was on the negotiating team on behalf of the city of Vukovar. And Ms. Vesna Bosanac would come to see him as well as Mr. Marin Vidic Bili, so we knew and we saw how the negotiations were going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you understand that in November towards the middle of November and later, that the evacuation was to take place pursuant to this agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were told that an agreement was signed with the Yugoslavia People's Army, that the city would surrender as I said a few minutes ago, and that all people, including the military and the police, would be allowed to leave the town of Vukovar and go wherever anyone wanted to go. At that point there was a confusion or rather panic, and people, and I was among them, went to the hospital. As I said, it was across the street from my shelter because, because, we believed that if there were more people, if there was a mass of people our chances were better, I mean our chances of survival, so that is exactly what we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what date was this that you went to the hospital? Can you remember that, the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 25th November 1991 in the evening, late in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say 25th; are you sure of that date or could it have been another date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is hard to tell exactly as far as dates are concerned, because the situation was such, then, that there was a lot of fear involved, so it is possible that it was the 25th or 26th November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- but what you are sure of is that it was the month of November.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you went to the hospital, what were the people fearful of, and what drove them to go to the hospital? What were they fearful of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People were not fearful of surrendering to the Yugoslavia People's Army, but they were fearful of surrendering to the paramilitary units, the so-called Chetniks, and rumour had it that they were committing atrocities around Vukovar in the villages that had fallen before the town of Vukovar itself. Therefore, people were fearful and they went to the hospital believing that their chances of survival were better if there were more people together en mass and that these people would be protected by the then Yugoslavia People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the hospital, what happened? What did you do when you got to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we came to the hospital we were followed by people, masses of people from all the shelters that were nearby in the centre of the town of Vukovar. We were told by the Red Cross, or rather by people who were involved in negotiations, that agreement was reached, that a list of people should be made according to buses, 50 or 55 people per bus, and that buses would come and take people out of the town of Vukovar and that is exactly what we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how long did you stay at the hospital for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in the hospital until 19th November 1991, around 5 pm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened on 19th November 1991 at 5 pm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were all expecting the arrival of representatives, or rather the arrival of the Yugoslavia People's Army and that is when they came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know who came? Who came from the people's Yugoslavia People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Officers came in camouflage uniforms, and one of them introduced himself by saying, "I am Major Sljivancanin. From now on you are going to obey my orders".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they do? What did these officers do when they arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they arrived, as I said, they said that, "from now on..." we would be listening to his orders and that we would be transported to a collection centre, as they called it, this collection centre being the storage space of Velepromet in Vukovar. We then realised that nothing would come out of the previous agreement reached.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was it that was to be transported to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said that first they would transport women, children and very old people, and then everyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say, "everybody else", or, "everyone else", did that include, so far as you know, the patients of the hospital, or did it only include the people who had gathered at the hospital for this evacuation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I think that everybody was supposed to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by what means were you to be evacuated from the hospital area over to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They evacuated us by military trucks from the hospital to Velepromet, namely to the yard of the Vupic enterprise which is across the street from the Velepromet storage area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there any other form of vehicles used apart from the military trucks? Did they have any other form of transport that you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were also some military APCs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, apart from Major Sljivancanin who you have spoken of, did you recognise any of the other military people that had arrived at the hospital yard on that day, 19th November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any local people who were dressed in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we went out into the yard, when we went out of the hospital building, I saw several persons, local people from Vukovar, who came to the Vukovar hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were transported to the -- to Velepromet, what happened when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were taken to Velepromet, namely myself and my group, we got off the trucks in the yard of Vupic. As I said, it was across the street from the Velepromet warehouse. There were already many people there who were brought in somehow from places and were simply left there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any stage while you were there see any buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what did they do with the people that arrived there in your group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived there or when we were arriving there there were individuals there, local people from Vukovar, among whom I knew quite a few. They were dressed in different types of uniforms. They were both men and women in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you recognise these uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you recognised them as?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were camouflage uniforms, there were old olive green/grey uniforms as we call them, those were the old military uniforms. There were people in civilian clothes, only with caps, there were all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you, in addition to that, see soldiers, regular soldiers of the Yugoslavia People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apart from those who had transported us, there were not any of them there then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, the people that you saw in uniform and in civilian clothes were people other than JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did these people who were dressed in military uniform other than JNA soldiers, do anything to the people that were getting out of these transport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is hard to describe the situation there at that moment, at that place that we were brought to. There was general confusion, general chaos. People were moaning, crying. There was shooting. There were people whom I knew and people whom I did not know, and it was night-time. They had torch lamps and they went from one person to another. They took away the people they wanted to take away to the places where they wanted to take them, so that is what happened to me too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say, "they took them away", you are talking about these people in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to ascertain, or did you know from your local knowledge, the ethnic background of these people that were dressed in these uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people I knew are the people whom I can recognise and I can claim that they were the people who were there, and of course, the people whom I did not know I cannot say what ethnic background they were. I knew the people who were locals from Vukovar and they were of Serb ethnic origin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it these people who were among those that were dressed in the military style of uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said a moment ago that they were taking people away. Were people being mistreated or maltreated anywhere around you when you first alighted from the buses and were first there, first arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that it was difficult to describe the situation that was there then. People were being taken away, beaten, in a way, maltreated in every possible way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that they took you away too. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know who it was that took you away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken away with a friend of mine who was with me. His name is Aleksandar Cotar, and we were taken out of the group by Darko Fot, and he took us to the other side, to the Velepromet yard, and he put us into a group by a big wall and that is where we stayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask what was happening at any stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked him because I knew him well. We were both hunters. So I asked him, "Darko, what is going on?". He said, "you will find out in good time".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you were put against the wall, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, people came to this wall, to this group of people who are standing by the wall. Again they used torch lights to light the faces of the people who were standing there, and then these people were taken away in an unknown direction. However, it was dark. There were no lights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they take you away or tell you to do something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I was taken out of this group by another man. His name was Mico Dankovic. I knew him personally, too. He was a waiter in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he do anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that a man was standing next to me. I know his name was Blaskovic and that he was a policeman in Vukovar. Mico Dankovic took him away, saying that they had certain things to settle from the past. He hit him with his rifle, he hit him on the face, and he cut his entire face that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What then happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took Blaskovic, and I did not realise at that point where he was taking him. After some time a third man came who took me out for the third time, and a man I remember, his name was called Jurica, and he worked in the catering enterprise in Vukovar. He said, "come here. You belong to me". This man's name was Boro Sujanovic and I knew him personally, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pausing for a moment there too, Blaskovic, you said he was a policeman, what was his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A Croat. From Sarengrad, a village near Ilok.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry, I interrupted you. Jurica said, "you are mine, come with me". What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Holding our arms he took us away into the dark and at one point I asked him, "Boro, where are you taking us?", and he replied – (redacted) (redacted). There is going to be a mess here tonight".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened then, after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took us in front of a small building which is somewhere in the middle of the storage area of Velepromet, and afterwards, when I walked in I realised that it was their workshop, their carpentry workshop, and in front of his workshop was a man wearing a camouflaged uniform without a cap. He had long black hair. He was very, very tall, and Boro, who brought us there, said, "Topola", he called him, "Topola, these guys are mine, so do not let anybody touch them". It was cold, so I was wearing a long denim overcoat, fur-lined, and I held a small bag in my hand with some personal belongings of my own and my wife's. I was ordered to put the bag aside, to take off my fur coat, and on that pile there were already quite a few bags and quite a lot of clothing. So I did that. After that, this same person, Topola, asked me to give my ID. I had a wallet and I took it out and I gave it to him, all of it. He opened it, he took the money out, he put it on the table that was in front of him, and there was already a small pile of money on that table, and he threw the documents and my wallet under the table. I remained standing there in a short leather jacket and he said, "take that off too, and put it on the pile there". When I did that, I told him, "give me back my ID, at least", and he answered, "you will never need that again. Stand over there". The same procedure followed. He did all of these same things with Jurica except that Jurica had German marks, I think, so this same person put the German marks in his pocket and he said, (redacted) (redacted). He opened the door -- it is a sliding door. You know, you open them this way (indicates), and he said, "get in". I walked in first and he kicked Jurica in the backside and he closed the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you got into that room what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was dark in the room at first, and then later on I could see in a corner there was a light and I observed that the room was filled with people. Some of these people -- and I later find out (redacted) (redacted) and they said, "what are you doing here?", and so I recognised the people who were there. This person who called me out and who was crouching next to the door is Mirko Blidovic, he is an investigator, he was actually an inspector for markets in the town of Vukovar. I also knew other people and I can mention several other names. There was a physician there who at that time worked in the Vukovar hospital. I think that his last name was Nadas. There was Petar Cicvaric who worked in the post office, and there was a man by the name of Zeko who worked for Velepromet. Then there were brothers, Molnar, I believe were their names, and there were other people who I knew from sight and whose names I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these people, like you, were being detained in this room, the people you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time during that evening when a person was thrown into the room who had been injured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A little before that, it is hard for me to pinpoint it, we heard burst of fire in front of the building where we were. After a while the door opened and a young man was thrown inside. His both legs were shot through. I know him by sight also. We tried to help him. At that moment this same physician, Nadas, who was there, tried it but we had nothing to help him with so I took my undershirt off, I gave it to Dr.Nadas so that he would stop his bleeding. However, we were not successful. At that moment I started banging at the door of this building and calling these men so that this person could be helped and indeed the door opened and this Topola person came in, and I told him that this man was bleeding and he was going to die. Soon thereafter two men showed up and they took him away. He was brought back about 10 minutes with his legs bandaged. We saw that this was done pretty well and we asked him, "Dragan, who bandaged you?". He said, "Dr.Maric did this".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after some time around about 9 pm in the evening, did someone then enter the room that you were detained in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After about 15, 20 minutes to half an hour, the door opened and a young man with blond -- with a beard showed up. He had a bottle in one hand, he had an automatic rifle on his chest. He was visibly inebriated, and he said, and I quote, "at 9.30 you are all going to be executed". That was it. He just closed the door and left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that we all fell silent. Our fear peaked, and indeed, around 9.30 the door opened of this room where we were, but the person who showed up at the door was not this blond man, but an officer of the JNA in the uniform with glasses. He had two soldiers by him with the same green/grey uniforms. At first, we thought that this was a firing squad. However, the men addressed us by saying, "people, get up." Up until then nobody called us anything else but Ustasha. We were surprised by his words and he continued, "take each other by the hands, two by two. Bow your heads. Do not look left or right. There is a bus waiting outside for you. Get on and sit down quietly. Nothing will happen to you". When we started taking each other by the hand, he told his soldiers, "turn around and whoever approaches, shoot". Outside there were people who were yelling, "kill Ustasha, do not take them anywhere". However, nobody approached us. So we entered the bus which indeed was in front of the building. The officer came on board. He said to the driver, "drive towards Negoslavci, and park behind a military vehicle called a peace carrier", and this is indeed what he did. After that, we watched from the bus. Immediately after that, we saw -- that is I saw -- that behind us other buses were lining up. I think there were seven or eight of them but I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you then taken to a camp where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started in the direction of Negoslavci, and I know this area so I know that we were going via Sid, and we reached Sremska Mitrovica. It was dark. We came to a stop in front of the prison in Sremska Mitrovica, and we remained there until the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when were you finally released? When did you finally go back to Croatia? What date, if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I went on 23rd of 1992. This was part of an exchange in Nemetin, near Osijek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 23rd of what month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of March. Of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I would ask you to look, if you would, for me, please, at a series of photographs, some you will not recognise, I will just ask you to pass over them. Those that you do recognise you may comment upon, but there is one particular photograph that I want to ask you about, so might the witness be shown the series of photographs in the binder entitled, "the route from Vukovar hospital".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder, would you mind if we take a recess now for twenty minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Not at all:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So we stand in recess now for twenty minutes. (11.00 am) (A short break) (11.20 am)

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness is brought back, if I may, would I just like to raise a matter in connection with this witness. In a moment I am about to show him an exhibit which we recovered from the scene in Ovcara and it is an object that he recognises and he will testify to. It is a very personal matter to him and he has asked me whether or not it is possible that he could have this artefact which will be shown in evidence. I have discussed it with my colleague, Mr. Fila, and he has very generously and kindly agreed that he would have no objection to it being photographed, after it has been actually tendered, to photograph it and then the witness in due course can be given this artefact, if your Honours have no objection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. (Witness returns to court).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown the book of photographs entitled, "route from Vukovar hospital", and perhaps it could be allocated a Prosecution exhibit number at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be allocated exhibit number 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness E, I have taken the liberty of actually marking with a yellow sticker the page of the photograph that I wish you to go to. For your Honour's -- the page is the 13th photograph in the booklet. Now, with the assistance of the overhead projector which we will have turned on in a moment I will get you to put that photograph on the screen beside you there. Could you do that? Do you see on that screen beside you there? Now, looking at the photograph on the projector but not on the television screen if you would, for me, please; Witness E, do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the barracks in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the JNA barracks, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to it, can you point to where Velepromet is, and point with a marker, if you would. The area of Velepromet. You may not be able to see it there but the area of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately to the right and another 5-600 metres ahead away from the barracks to the right on the right-hand side of the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So it is not clearly shown on that photograph. Perhaps that might be returned --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no you cannot see it. You cannot see it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will not seek to tender that, your Honour, at this stage, if it could just be marked for identification and a subsequent witness will go through it in greater detail. Now, Witness E, you are a married man. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had two children, a boy and a girl.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time of the conflict -- when was your boy born?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his first name? Just his first name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Josip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time of the conflict that you have testified about in your evidence, what was your son doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a member of the defence of the city of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see him during the course of the conflict from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he from time to time come to the shelter that you were in when you were in Vukovar during the siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Both my wife and I were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your son visit you occasionally when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw your son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 19th November at the time when I was departing from Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw him at the hospital, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he doing at the hospital when you saw him on the last occasion, on the very last occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Together with other people he had duty to transport the seriously wounded from the Vukovar hospital. He was part of the transportation and escort group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen him since that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, no. After that, since then, I have not seen him. After 19th, between 4 and 5 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make enquiries as to what may have happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After my departure from the hospital I was taken to the camp in Stajicevo and then to the Sremska Mitrovica camp. The International Red Cross came and of course I tried to enquire about him, but there was not a single word, nothing, that I could find out about his whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, any time from that time or not, November 1991 to this present, obtain any information about what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received different kinds of information. Some were to the effect that he was in prison in the Republic of Serbia. Other information was that they were all killed in Vukovar, at Ovcara, and various other types of information which all unfortunately proved incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would ask you to look at this object that is now shown to you, or two objects that are now shown to you. Would you please, when you receive them, take them out of the bag and place them on the overhead projector so we can see: if the overhead projector can be set up, please, to receive them. Spread them out when you put them there, please, Witness E: Now, looking at those two objects that you now see on the screen, Witness E, do you recognise those at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a silver chain that my son had on with a little plaque on it where it says, "God and Croats". The other pendant is a golden clover. This was a gift from my daughter Ivana, who lives with me. This is a statue of Saint Anthony given to him by my wife in the hope that it would protect him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was the last time that you saw these artefacts that are now on the screen, before coming here to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see these items except in Zagreb when I went to identify them and the last time we saw them was on him in the hospital in Vukovar, and that is how we identified him.

utterances.speaker: MR.  NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender those, your Honours. And your Honours, might I make an application on behalf of the witness? He has requested me that they be photographed and that he could recover the originals and if your Honours please, Mr. Fila has indicated he has no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Cross-examined by MR. FILA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies to you, sir. It is difficult for me too at this moment. Witness E, how far is the police station in a straight line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you know, was there any bullets fired from it at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies again for having to ask some questions regarding your son, I know it is very difficult.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Go ahead and ask.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was taken out on the 19th or the 20th from the hospital, based on the stories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 20th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that anyone of those who were taken out on 18th or 19th ended up at Ovcara, that is ended up being killed at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your testimony you mentioned the name of Darko Fot. Is he a Serb or Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was from a mixed marriage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, Fot is a Croatian name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a mixed marriage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Mirko Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he was from a mixed marriage too. I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am asking you this because when you were there, mistreated by the paramilitary, were there just Serbs there or Croats there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mentioned the names that I know. As far as I know, he was from the mixed marriage but most of them were Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there were others, too; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In closing, I would just like to ask you one more question and not use any more time. You said that you had some kind of trust in -- and in the end it was a JNA officer who saved you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You recognised the locals from Vukovar in the paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these people who could take the military around and show them where everything was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, they did not need any third party to go and show them where the hospital was, and other facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, I would like to -- this is my last question and my apologies for having to ask these questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Nothing in re-examination, your Honours. I do not know whether the exhibited has been given an exhibit number, but...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, number 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one question. Witness E, I have one question. In your witness statement you said that, when you said, and I quote: "When we got to Velepromet, JNA soldiers started to divide people in four groups. Women were in one group, Serbs in the second group, Croats in the third fourth and known Croats in the fourth group." Now, my question is, what do you mean by, "known Croats", in the fourth group? Who made up this fourth group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, before the war there were about 23 ethnic groups and nationalities living in Vukovar. When we were taken from the hospital to Velepromet, we all had to identify ourselves according to the ethnic group, and we were divided accordingly. That means that the Croats, or, as we were popularly called then, the Ustasche, would be separated one side, the Serbs on the other and then the Ruthinians, Ukrainians and Hungarians and others made the third group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Fourth group. Yes. Thank you. Any objection to the witness being released?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection? Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may now be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, too. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I assume the Prosecution is going to call the next witness, witness number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for not referring by his name, because this witness would also like protection, and the Defence has kindly agreed to that. His name will be Witness O. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I would like to ask Witness O to make the solemn declaration. WITNESS O (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Examined by MR. WAESPI

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning. According to your wishes, witness, your name will not be disclosed, so you are now Witness O. I will have you shown a piece of paper with your name on it, and please look at it and just indicate by saying, "yes", or, "no", whether you see your name on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please show it to the Defence, and I would like to tender that under seal, and it is probably going to be Prosecution exhibit number 22.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness O, do you remember having been interviewed in April 1996 by an investigator from this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you sign a document which was the English translation of this interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like the usher, again, to show him a document, and it comes with the Croatian translation. I would like you, Witness O, to tell us whether you see your signature on the document on the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to tender it now, together with the Croatian translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 23, Croatian translation, 23A.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you comfortable, Witness O?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am an economist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you still working now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am retired, but I will work again because I am needed at the hospital when the adequate facilities are found.
