utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please outline for us your educational background and especially your work experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had difficult times during education. I was orphaned during World War II and when I started the secondary school I basically remained in the street because the people who had adopted me, the woman who adopted me died, so I put myself through school alone, by myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that your main experience in work as a professional was carried out in the Vukovar hospital for three decades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991 were you still employed in the Vukovar hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, although until the fall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the nature of your job? What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the war I was not working in supplies department, I think, between August and October I was involved, in fact -- there were about 30 men who were husbands of the female physicians and nurses and they were part of a group that worked in providing oxygen tanks and moving the wounded and cleaning and all kinds of manual labour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, but your main job before the war, let us say in 1990, was, you were in charge of providing supplies, general supplies, within the hospital. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was at first in charge of supplies. That means that I had under me the department for providing food and all medical supplies and various inventory. That was all part of my job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, turning to these final days before the fall of Vukovar, you said you were sort of involved into food providing, preparation. Can you tell us for how many people you prepared the food in those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For about 700 people. These were both patients and hospital staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Where were you living at that time? In the hospital? And if so, since when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I lived at the hospital. After August I was not going home any more because my home was destroyed. I was -- the conditions were very difficult and I myself would lie and sleep under the patients' beds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the hospital ever directly targeted? Do you recall such incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was fired at non-stop, and I am trying to remember. It was, I think, in the October when two so-called, "hogs", were fired at the hospital. It landed and it passed through all the floors and it did not explode. The other one exploded in the hospital yard and inflicted a lot of damage to both the old and the new buildings of the hospital. In other words, it was horrible because it broke down the doors, windows, and in the middle of the hospital there was a sign which measured 20 by 20, and also on the roof there was a sign that it was a hospital. I can also say that at times up to 4,000 shells were falling on the hospital in a single day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the hospital defended? Were there any weapons in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the hospital did not defend itself. There were no weapons, but at the reception desk there were guards and also at the entrance to the wards there were two guards. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you informed at some point by the hospital management that you would be leaving in a convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Dr.Vesna Bosanac -- well, I am not sure whether this was 18th or 19th in the evening, she went to see all the employees at all the departments. She said that Vukovar had fallen and that everyone would be allowed to go where they pleased. Whoever wanted to go to Croatia, whoever wanted to go to Serbia would go to Serbia. That was the agreement reached.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day you just mentioned, the day you were informed about being evacuated, was there any more fighting going on? (12.00)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not really. From afar you could hear shooting but the actual fighting had ceased. You could hear burst of gunfire from afar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened now in the early morning of November 20th? Were you preparing breakfast?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Early in the morning the food department was preparing breakfast for all the wounded and for the staff, and behind us was a soldier with a machine-gun. This was very unpleasant to us and he was monitoring every step we made so it was quite unpleasant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At a certain time now, did one of the hospital staff members inform you that you had to leave now the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was between 9 o'clock and 9.30. I do not know if it was a cleaning woman or a nurse, I really do not know, but somebody came to call us because we were much farther from the crisis staff in the hospital and the hospital staff than others because this was a special department for food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you directed to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were directed to the entrance for emergencies through the shelter. We were met there by soldiers, regular soldiers, not paramilitary units. They stood in a line and they checked all our personal belongings and then we boarded the buses. I entered the last bus, the fifth bus and it was crowded. There were over 60 people on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were these other 60 people you had just mentioned? Were they civilians, patients? Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The other people, there were paramilitaries and civilians. How should I put this? I think they are paramilitary units too. Those were our local Serbs who entered the yard. They entered the hospital yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talk about paramilitaries, you talk about the soldiers you saw outside in the hospital yard. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the hospital yard I saw paramilitary units too. They were not the army. They were -- well, how should I put it? Paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when you talk about the passengers in the buses, or in the bus, you boarded, the last one, the fifth one, who were those other passengers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The other passengers were wounded people with lighter wounds, some civilians and also technical staff from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall some of the names of those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who were on the bus, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Adaga Jozo, Zeljko Jozo, Varenica Franjo, Fradic Tomo, Sven Juro, Jarabik Slatko, Bajndrauch Ivan, Gavric and others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there only men on this bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only in that bus, but on all the buses there were men only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what kind of buses those were? Civilian? Military? The colour of it, maybe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they were olive green, of very poor quality with wooden seats on the bus. Those were real military vehicles, I imagine, for going out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did those buses, specially your bus, pull off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately around 10 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told which direction or which aim this bus would have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I personally thought it was some kind of routine check. We were not informed as to where we were going but I simply thought that we were going for a routine check of some kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which route now did the bus take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bus went along Gunduliceva Street through the centre of town but on the right-hand side towards the military barracks, then we crossed the bridge, then by the orthodox church up towards the health centre, towards Velepromet, and then we turned to the barracks and that is where they stopped us and they parked the buses in a semicircle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned that you passed by the Velepromet. How far away is Velepromet from the JNA barracks, your final goal of the trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About a kilometre, a kilometre and a half away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what did happen at the JNA barracks? Did the buses stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The buses stopped and after that paramilitaries started coming in from all sides. Arkanovci, Seseljovci and the local Chetniks, rather, Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe their mood? How were they acting? Were they quiet, were they organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in a terrible mood. How shall I put this? They were euphoric. Most of them took out knives. They threatened us. They had beards that I have the feeling that they had not taken a bath for two months. They had encircled the buses and they were threatening that they would kill us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did then an officer come into the bus and ask for the names of a number of doctors, like a certain Dr.Farkas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A higher officer walked in and he asked for Dr.Farkas and Dr.Emedi and Dr.Simunovic and Mr. Esterajher, a journalist, and Sinisa Glavasevic, a journalist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now this officer, this higher ranking officer you just described, do you think he was one of those paramilitaries who were walking, running around, the paramilitaries you said who were threatening you, or was he from another unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He was simply a military person with a high rank, not to say a very high rank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he behave? Was he more friendly than the other soldiers you had just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He behaved in a fair manner. He simply came and asked us whether we knew where these people were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did somebody know on the buses who were these people were, he asked for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally knew about Dr.Farkas, Dr.Emedi, and Dr.Simunovic, because naturally I had worked with them and I knew that all three of them were in Borovokomerc but naturally I did not want to say so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after the officer had left and while you were still waiting in the bus, did at a certain time Rudolf Wilhelm or somebody else on the bus recognise one of the soldiers whom you had just described as being circling around the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not say with certainty that this was Rudolf Wilhelm, but judging by his voice I knew him. I thought it was him but I knew this same person too, but I had hidden because during his free time he worked with Neso, this other person from the warehouse and when Rudolf appealed to him for help and said, "save us", he answered, "I cannot help you in any way. The people who are on Neso's list are done in for". Neso is an abbreviation, a nickname for Nedjelvko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened next? Did another soldier, a higher ranking one, board the bus with a list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He boarded the bus with a list, and he called out five or six people from each bus, so about 30 of us were called out. We were called out and we had to get off the bus and a new bus was there, about 50 metres away, prepared for us, and we walked there and in the meantime these paramilitaries were lined up and they had iron bars and wooden bars and they were hitting us as we were walking as much as they could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You just mentioned a list. Were you also on that list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My name was called out too and I was second or third on the list that was called out on my bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were also relatives of you mentioned on that list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My brother and my nephew, who were also employed in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find out later who may have put your names on that list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is how it went. When we were taken away, rather kidnapped, that is a better word, because Sljivancanin had a meeting with the medical staff and in the meantime they were taking us away, the men, those who were not medical staff but who belonged to the technical staff, and at the very last moment a nurse walked out. Oh, I cannot remember her name right now. Well, it is not important. A nurse who saw her husband and she said, "people, I am getting suspicious. Our men are being taken away in an unknown direction", and then nurse Mokos, who worked at surgery, asked Dr.Ivankovic to ask Mr. Sljivancanin to make a list, saying that we were employees of the hospital, that we did not have weapons, that we did not participate in the war and that we should be withdrawn. That was done, so my wife put my name on the list and my nephew's name and also the names of my friends who had worked with me for years, but unfortunately I think that a certain restriction was made already in the hospital, so not all the people from that list were called out. That is to say that in the hospital they decided this person is okay, this person is not. I think that this was done by the fifth column that was present in the hospital and they made this decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that you were taken out of this bus into another bus. Were in this other bus again soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were two local paramilitaries, Chetniks, one Bulic Milan and the other one I do not know personally. He is from Negoslavci and in the front of the bus itself there was a young soldier, 20-ish, perhaps, and I had the feeling that he had arrived in the army only a day or two before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you beaten by these soldiers you had just mentioned in this bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat us terribly with iron bars. All of us. But Zelvko Jozo the most. Bulic Milan hit him with an iron bar. He hit him on the head, and also he kicked him in the face, and he fell, and he said, "Milan, are you doing this? How many lunches and dinners did you have at my place?", because they were personal friends before the war, because his wife worked with him in the hospital kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Obviously, these soldiers sort of had some conversation with you. Did they also threaten you, besides beating you? Did they threaten you with words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They threatened, saying that they were taking us to be executed as the bus was leaving, but they were saying this only to frighten us. They said that they were taking us to be executed, but that was not true. They just wanted to intimidate us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember names of those people who were now with you on the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do remember some, Wilhelm Zvonimir, Vlaho Miroslav, Vlaho Marko, Kolesar Mihovil, Danko, I do not know his name, Danko is his last name, then... I cannot remember right now. There were about 30 of us. Adaga Jozo, Zeljko Jozo and others. I did not know only one person there. I did not know his name or surname. He worked at Jugopetrol, at the bus station and they were saying that he had killed Jovo Rakijica, he was killed, but that was not true. We were accused, we who were on the bus, that we had slaughtered 50 children as Ustashas which was not true. That was denied only a few days later. An Italian woman journalist had written this. I do not know how, and this was released throughout the world, but in a few days it was denied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know these people you had just mentioned being with you on the bus well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, except for this man whom they said killed Jovo Rakijica. I had only seen him from time to time, but these other people I knew personally and I was even friends with some of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. For how long did you stay in this JNA compound until you left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately three-quarters of an hour or an hour, not more than that, but only we, these 30 men I mentioned and the remaining buses stayed on at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now were you told this time where your bus was heading to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They said that they were taking us to Anica to be executed but that was not true. They were only frightening us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where did the trip eventually go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They brought us to the back entrance to the hospital in Gunduliceva Street, some in front of the hospital. We were supposed to get off there, but the local Serbs who worked with us were supposed to guarantee that we did not have any weapons and that we worked at the hospital. Some of the nurses got their husbands out, some of the doctors got their husbands out and I asked two doctors who did not refuse, but they did not come, so accidentally Ms. Bosanac showed up and she went to Sljivancanin when she saw us and she asked Mr. Sljivancanin to release us, which is what he did. So I, my brother and my nephew got off. Zeljko Jozo and Adaga Jozo remained on the bus, crying, and they asked me to talk to the head of the food department, a lady, and to go, to ask her to go to Mr. Sljivancanin and to let them go too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they also able to get off the bus, those two people you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They could not leave. Somebody had to guarantee for them and ask that they be released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they released, eventually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not. As soon as I got off the bus I addressed Anica Sila, who was head of the food department. I asked her to go to Mr. Sljivancanin and to ask him and my wife went too and Zeljko Dragica, Zeljko Jozo's wife. She was about 50 metres away from them, and they addressed Mr. Sljivancanin who said, "wait. Now we are going to take care of this". In the meantime a man, paramilitary Chetnik with a beard walked up to him, asked him to come to the other side, whispered something to him, and gave Dragica a terrible look and then Sljivancanin said, "go, if they are guilty they will be punished and if they are not guilty they are going to be released". Unfortunately they were not released. I know that one of them has been identified and buried already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay there at the hospital in the yard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the hospital yard I did not stay there very long. I simply went to the other street through the hospital where there was a convoy with the wounded and medical staff and the European Monitors were there. They had -- I do not know what. White flags or something. There were quite a few vehicles, the European Monitors were there, and buses for the medical staff, and ambulances with the heavily wounded on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe these buses for us? Were they the same with which you came and you described earlier as being olive grey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite frankly, I do not remember. I think they were a bit more comfortable, but since I did not even get to see the seats, I cannot tell. I, for example had to stand all the way because we were packed like sardines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was on that bus? Do you remember people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were people, medical staff mostly. My wife was there. I know that Ms. Cakalic was there, who did not belong to the hospital. That is the wife of a colleague who used to work at the hospital, and the rest were all employees of the hospital; nurses, doctors, medical technicians, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these hospital staff members wearing white coats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the convoy?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, in the buses when in the convoy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. They were wearing civilian clothes and we all had white overcoats when we were taken to the military barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when did your bus start to move and into what direction was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our bus started to move some time between 2 and 3 pm. We went along the main street, Ive Lole Rebara and we turned by the pharmacy and then we turned to the street -- actually we went straight through the centre of the town then we went through Radiceva Street and then we turned to Senoina Street. From Senoina we turned to the right towards the cemetery. We reached a cross-roads then we turned to the left, towards the health centre, or rather towards Velepromet and Modateks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stop at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We stopped there for a short while. From the windows we saw that there were a lot of prisoners in the yard, then Dr.Maric showed up. He waved to us, and we, all the employees of the hospital, turned our heads away from him in protest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is Dr.Maric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr.Maric was an orthopaedic specialist. As soon as the war broke out he went I do not know where, to Negoslavci or to Bobota, to the clinic there. He no longer worked at the hospital. And, as far as I found out, he was a colonel in the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Montenegrin, I think, but I am not sure. A Serb or a Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were just waiting a few moments, you said, I think, a short time, at Velepromet. Afterwards, into what direction did you move on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started moving towards Modateks and they were driving us around and finally they took us to Negoslavci because they told us that they were negotiating with the Croat government and then they said that allegedly Tudjman did not want us, which was not true, and they did not know what to do with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you drive from Vukovar on the main road to Negoslavci or did you use any detours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We took a detour. We took a village by-roads which slowed down the evacuation itself. I guess this was part of their psychological torture, because they kept telling us, "Tudjman does not want you. We do not know what to do with you". Things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the pace of that convoy was rather slow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rather slow. That was intentional. They intentionally slowed it down. That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there lots of traffic on those roads you were taking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was no traffic at all. We only saw in the villages through which we passed from nearly every backyard of a house tanks were pointing their turrets, their barrels in various directions. (12.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any checkpoints? Were you stopped on the way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As far as I recall, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it already dark when you reached Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After Negoslavci, did you continue on the road to Orolik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We went in the direction of Orolik, and I do not recall exactly where they took us after that, but we ended up in Sremska Mitrovica. In Sremska Mitrovica the European Monitors registered us and told us not to move, to listen to them, even though the soldiers had insisted that we go to a large hall we, however, we decided to listen to the European Monitors and even though we spent practically the entire night on a single foot, crammed in the buses, that is where we stayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One final question. Was the road between Negoslavci and Orolik any different to the road you had been travelling before in terms of traffic and road condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was clear and it was almost intact, and when we moved there at that time it was just potholes next to one another, and so we barely moved along.

utterances.speaker: MR.  WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila? Cross-examined by MR. FILA

utterances.speaker: MR.  FILA
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The record reflects that you passed Velepromet from the hospital to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was to the right. To the left was the barracks and to the right is the Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what comes first, so you could not have passed Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but they took us there but then they took us to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Then it is fine. That is then correct, what you said. In your statement you said that on 19th November some Bojan Kuzmic took out Ivan Bozak and then Marko Mandic. This was on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, yes. Yes, that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. As well as Marko Vlaho?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marko Vlaho stayed alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know what happened to Ivan Bozak and Marko Mandic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Marko Mandic was taken in an unknown direction and he still has not been identified and as far as Bozak is concerned I know that he was killed in front of the hospital. Personally did I not see this, but a female janitor saw this and I mentioned that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies. This person is in the indictment as if he was killed at Ovcara. This Ivan Bozak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me try to answer that question. When we arrived in Zagreb all the hospital employees were given work duty with the Red Cross of Croatia to help compile lists but since we knew all the personnel, all the staff, since the families were already searching for their own members, so that this hospital staff was also being looked for and I knew this, even Bozak. I did not say to anyone that he was killed, but I personally put him down on the list so that he would not disappear, but I know that he was not killed on Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The reason for my asking this was not to question your testimony but rather to point to the indictment. You said in your testimony that in May many Serbs from Borovo Selo were brought who were shot by the dum-dum bullets and that you were affected by that. Would you elaborate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At that time I was in my office and I received a message that in Borovo Selo there was shooting going on and that all ambulances should be sent over there because there were wounded. I informed the chief of the transportation unit and he sent the vehicles and I also put my vehicle to their disposal, the vehicle that belonged to my department, and I also wanted to personally go there. He told me, "do not go, wait for me and if necessary, be ready to provide some assistance". When they came back I was shocked because indeed there were massacred. They looked terrible. It looked horrible. I am not a medical expert, but I felt horrible, and since I was orphaned, I had lost both my parents, who were killed by the Chetniks during World War II, so I was in a state of shock because I realised that we had a -- repeated events and I was -- I spent 20 days in a Europe psychiatric ward and lost 20 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you know personally the hospital staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I showed you a videotape of some buses with people on board, could you recognise certain persons if they were your hospital staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With your permission your Honours, and if there are no objections by the Prosecutor, we would like to replay the same tape that is the Defence exhibit number 2. Meanwhile, did the military give out tea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, only in Mitrovica when we stepped out at one point. That was in Serbia were we given some tea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said it was about 2, 2.30 when you were at Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, about that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, obviously that was an approximation. There was no situation to know the exact time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you recognise anyone, please do say so. (Video played)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is our nurse with her daughter who worked at a maternity ward. This is at Velepromet. This is Vesna Vrancic with her daughter. This is Seremet, I do not know her first name, and her daughter-in-law, Vaber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the bus, when you see people on the buses, can you tell us if you recognise anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Hadzic. Hadzic again. Arkan. This is Terek, and this is the janitor in the -- the cleaning lady, so I recognise Marija Terek on the bus who worked as an administrator in the department for hygiene and disease control, and the other one was a cleaning lady. I do not know what department she worked on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to tell you, to ask you, was this on the 20th? Are these -- the bus is from the 20th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the people who were being evacuated from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, you have different things. A little bit of Velepromet, a little bit of this, so this is an edited tape, so I do not know what to tell you. I think that something is not right. There is a bus there which was leaving, that is where Miss Terek and this cleaning lady was, but there were more buses. I would recognise at least some people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this a bus from the convoy or the bus which went on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on -- on the convoy because Miss Terek left together with me on the convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this on the 20th, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is an amateur tape. You are aware of that. We are just trying to identify...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies. I am not sure this is part of the convoy because this could have been in Velepromet, it could have been transferred from Modateks, I cannot guarantee this because several things are spliced together so it is unclear because the hospital staff were separate from the wounded. There were several buses so here you have a little bit of Velepromet and a little bit of another piece of tape where I recognise two persons, so it does not mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It does not matter that you do not recognise it. Was it on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say. I do not know whether this person have been -- were taken prisoner somewhere else and then transported later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this on the same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that. My colleague Miss Terek I recognised her. She was leaving on the 20th together with me.

utterances.speaker: MR.  FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is what I needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Re-examination? Re-examination by MR. WAESPI

utterances.speaker: MR.  WAESPI
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions. First of all, you just said that there was something not right with that tape. Do you want to see it again to tell us more specifically what you doubt about this tape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What bothers me is that Velepromet was put in there and then only one bus in which I recognised these two persons, one cleaning lady and this administrator in the department for disease control, so you have a little bit of the Velepromet and a little bit of... as far as I know, neither Arkan or Hadzic were at the hospital and now I see them there, so it is all mixed up, so I... Personally, I did not know, I never saw him nor did I hear that he was ever at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me come back to other points Mr. Fila asked you. The first one, he asked you if these were Serbs shot at Borovo Selo, and you said that these were Serbs that had been shot, I am just taking it from the transcript. Is that what you were answering to Mr. Fila's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is the answer, but I cannot say with certainty that if there were not some local people from Vukovar whom I did not recognise. As far as I know, none of our people were killed, so I assumed that these were the Serbs because this was in Borovo Selo. Because all of our staff returned with ambulances and they brought back the seriously wounded, so I did not recognise a single local from Vukovar and a single Croat in that convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you personally -- you were not aware of any Croats being shot in Borovo Selo also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that they were executed but they were not brought to the hospital because if they had been executed then they were not taken to the hospital because as far as I know the rule is that you do not bring back dead bodies. You just bring back the wounded people who may -- can be helped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Croatian policemen shot there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I heard that. I never saw it or experienced it. I heard that the policemen were killed at the very entrance to Borovo Selo and in Borovo Selo itself. This is what I have heard so I cannot claim anything with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR.  WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. One moment please, your Honours. (Pause). No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask two questions of the witness. Now, you told us that you came across two groups of military people, so one consisted of JNA officers or soldiers and the other were local, as you say, you said, "local paramilitary". Now, my first question is as follows; when you were beaten up, I understand that you were beaten up by so-called, "local", paramilitary people at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were being beaten up, were there any JNA officers there present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was only one soldier who probably had just arrived. It was just a regular soldier who must have been mobilised just prior to that. He was about 20 years old, but I would like to make a correction. I did not see military personnel in those groups. They were the Arkan people and the Seselj people and the locals. They were all paramilitary of whom I thought, you see, they are honest, they did not take part in this war, but they all showed up at this barracks. The people that I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, my second question is more general. Judging from what you saw, what sort of relationship was there between the JNA officers or soldiers and the paramilitary people? Were the JNA people in command or in control of the paramilitary or not, or vice versa, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all. They simply pretended not to see these atrocities and there were not many of them. They simply did not want to see what was being done. They sort of tried to distance themselves. They did not say, "do not do this", but simply allowed that they do these atrocities to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any objection to the witness being released?

utterances.speaker: MR.  FILA
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much for coming. You may be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We stand now in recess until 2.30 sharp. The hearing is adjourned. (1.50 pm) (Luncheon adjournment) 24 25 (2.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether the Prosecution would like to call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR.  WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes your Honour, we are prepared to. We have spoken previously with this witness and he has indicated that he did not wish protective measures but my colleague Mr. Waespi is checking with the witness right now to see if that is still the case and as soon as he returns, we will be ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether I could ask the Prosecution whether they have handed in the statements of Witness K and witness number 15. So witness 11 and witness 15 on the preliminary list of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR.  WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to witness 15, no statement was taken from that individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Oh yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.  WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And in relation to witness 11 I believe it may have already been provided but with his real name. I am checking that, and perhaps in the break this afternoon I can verify that and I can report back to the court. If not, then we can provide copies later this afternoon for both the court and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR.  WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Just a moment, your Honour. (Pause). Your Honour, the next witness has requested image alteration but other than that, everything else is fine, so he will be testifying under his real name and there will be no voice alteration necessary. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. May I ask the witness to make the solemn declaration? HAJDAR DODAJ (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Examined by MR. WILLIAMSON

utterances.speaker: MR.  WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Sir, could you state your name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HAJDAR Dodaj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Dodaj, where are you from originally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Dakovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you lived there most of your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you live, growing up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bjelovar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the address.

utterances.speaker: MR.  WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And what is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Albanian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point in time, were you obligated to go to the JNA for your national service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 18th March 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Dodaj, if you can just lean up a little bit and speak closer to the microphone, I think the interpreter is having a little difficulty in hearing you. When you went into the JNA on March 18th of 1991 where were you sent initially?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Petrovac Na Mlavi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is that located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is in Serbia, near Pozarevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the military unit to which you were assigned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mechanised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you entered the military was your unit composed of persons from all of the Yugoslav republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any differentiation in treatment based on where soldiers were from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were soldiers from different areas treated differently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We who were from Croatia had to work harder than those who were from Serbia. They had more favourable conditions than we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this apply to soldiers who came from other republics as well or was it only limited to Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, especially for Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of 1991 did you see a decrease in the number of soldiers who were coming from other areas of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were not coming from Slovenia or from Croatia then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of some of the tensions that existed between Serbia and Croatia or between Serbia and Slovenia during this time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told anything about what was happening by your superior officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they said that there was a group of people... I do not know how to put this. A group of people who were rebelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point did you try to leave the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was running away. I escaped from the barracks in June and then they caught me in Zemun again and then they took me back to Pozarevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you punished as a result of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what punishment did you receive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 60 days of military imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point thereafter was your unit deployed to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it sent to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In July, Bjelo Brdo by Osijek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when your unit went to Bijelo Brdo, what tasks were you given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we received the task of destroying about 20,000 Ustasha in Zedlosdo and the villages around Osijek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge was there 20,000 Ustasha in the villages around Osijek?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not a single one, no. These were people who were defending their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did your unit remain in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 20 days. We spent about 20 days in that place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then they took us back to Petrovac Na Mlani, back to the military barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point were you sent back to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time what were you told about where you were going or what you would be doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not told anything. We were not told where we were taken, 10 or 20 soldiers were selected, most of them from Croatia and then we were sent to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Sremska Mitrovica were you told what you would be doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We were told. We got all our equipment, our war weapons, et cetera, and we went to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, by September of 1991 when you were arriving in Mitrovica, had the composition of the military forces changed even more in terms of ethnic breakdown than it was before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. There was more hatred. There was more hatred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there more Serbs in the military than there had been previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the numbers of Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were very few of them. Very few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Slovenes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were not any Slovenes, not a single one, because they all went back to their republic. They were taken back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the additional Serbs come from that were in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Reservists were coming in. There was mobilisation then in Serbia. They were volunteers from all parts of Serbia. They came from all parts of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this also include soldiers from Territorial Defence units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, a moment ago you said that there was more hatred in the army. Can you explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they said that they could hardly wait to reach Vukovar to destroy all the Croatian people, to simply destroy everything that was Croatian. They played Serbian songs to us...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it appear to you to still be a truly Yugoslav army at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it did not seem that to me any more. When I saw that these were reservists and they did not have the insignia of the Yugoslav army, they had Serbian flags and they had the Kokarda sign, et cetera, they had the Serbian flag. It was the Serbian flag that we had, rather than the Yugoslavia flag.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any point in time did you encounter any Serb paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Negoslavci I saw them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know which groups these forces were affiliated with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was their role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the same as ours, to destroy the entire city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these paramilitary forces appear to be co-operating closely with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it seemed so, that they were co-operating because in Negoslavci they had this crisis staff of theirs, the Territorial Defence and the Yugoslavia army was with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your unit engaged in any fighting in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you able to observe in terms of the way that the battle was being conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We came on the 1st September, the position between Luzac and Bogdanovci. That is on the road between Vinkovci and Vukovar so we had cut that road and we dug in there with our tanks and transporters and then we were shooting at the city with everything we had available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What types of weaponry was the JNA using?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this unit of mine used tanks. 100 millimetre tanks, and 20 millimetre transporters and PKT automatic rifles and small arms and mortars, 60 and 80 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see JNA aircraft being used against Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On 14th September 1991 I saw them, when they shelled the city with five or four aircraft.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also see heavy artillery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I saw that too. Cannons...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tanks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tanks? That unit of mine at that point had about 20 tanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often was the city shelled by the JNA forces and the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Day and night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was continuous?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, only when we would go to have breakfast or lunch then we would take a break about one hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any orders in regard to what was being targeted in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, with tanks, you know, we mostly used tanks to fire at the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you targeting anything in particular in the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any instructions given as to certain areas being places that you should hit or other places that you should not hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nobody looked at that. We were simply shelling the city regardless of whether these were military targets or civilian or something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of resistance was coming from the Croatian forces that were defending the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very little resistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Croats have aircraft?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have artillery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not have any kind of heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have tanks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell anything about the level of destruction that was occurring in the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, everything was being destroyed in town and around town. All civilian houses, big buildings, the water works, all of that was happening from our positions. While I was in the army, every day we fired about 100-200 shells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just from your unit alone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our unit alone, but then there were other units too but then I did not see these units. I know about my unit because I was still in the army then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you decided that you would try to escape from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you by yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was the fifth soldier to escape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did all of you actually go about getting away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were together most of the time, and that is how we agreed on that, that we should escape from that army and join the Croat army or the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were you able to accomplish this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 24th September around 12 o'clock we simply set off for certain houses that were on neutral territory, it was a neutral zone. There were not any civilians there. We said we would go to these houses to get something, you know, so that we would not be cold, so that is how we left our positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when you got to these houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, then we encountered a civilian and we asked him to go to the guard and to tell them that there were five soldiers there who were on the run and who wanted to surrender and then the Croatian soldiers took us in. They treated us kindly. We were all all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were driven away to Vukovar to the police station in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after you arrived at the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they welcomed us there. We took off our uniforms, we were given civilian clothes and we were there in the police station, we were questioned as to whether there were other people from Croatia there, whether there were any Croats in the army and whether they wanted to escape too, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you made it to the Croatian side did it appear to you that the town was occupied by Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was people who were from that town only. They were defending their homes with whatever they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this consistent with what your officers in the JNA had been telling you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had they been telling you in terms of who you were fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the JNA?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were telling us that we were fighting against the Ustashas, against mercenaries who came from elsewhere. Mostly against the Ustashas, that is what they told us, that we were fighting against them, and we were actually supposed to fight against the Croat people rather than Ustashas. I did not see any Ustashas there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were able to see first hand what the Croats had to fight with in terms of weapons and manpower, would you say that the Serb forces and the Croatian forces were evenly matched?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, not at all, because the Serb side had heavy weapons, aviation and the Croat side had hunting rifles, pistols, small calibre guns, hardly anybody had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you join the Croatian forces in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any Serbs fighting with the Croats, defending Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some Serbs also fought against the army, the Serb army, I mean in the defence of Vukovar. In Vukovar, you know, there were different nationalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you were in the city itself were you able to see more closely the damage that the city had sustained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw quite a bit of damage in town. There was hardly a single building that had not been shelled with at least a few shells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any buildings which seemed to be particularly hard hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were, yes. Yes. There were. I mean, the hospital, too. I was in the hospital pretty often so I saw what was happening there. They were shooting at it from aircraft, also from tanks from all sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were at the hospital on various occasions did you observe anything which indicated to you that it was a military target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not. I did not notice anything. It was not a military target. It was a civilian target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point in time did it become apparent to you that the battle was nearing an end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes, yes, towards the end. They had already occupied the entire city and you could not get out of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was this, as the battle was coming to a close?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, 17th November, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go at the end of the battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 18th November 1991 I came to the hospital because I thought that was the safest place. I thought nothing would happen to me there so a colleague of mine and I came there, although there were quite a few people there, civilians, wounded people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the situation at the hospital when you arrived? Were there many people there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were quite a few people there, about 450 wounded, and then also civilians and women and children and old people. All of them were at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take your weapon with you to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. We were not allowed to carry the weapons into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a point in time when you became aware of the fact that the JNA had arrived at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The JNA came and the Territorial Defence and the volunteers, all their military formations, so the soldiers from all different formations were coming to the hospital and around the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when the JNA arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 19th they separated the women and children and they took them some place, I do not know where, while the men were kept in hospital and then on 20th around 9 o'clock, 8.30, 9 o'clock, they lined us up in front of the hospital, and then the buses arrived, they loaded up on to these buses and took us to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, just going back a little bit, what was going on in the hospital on the night between the 19th and the 20th November.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what happened there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During that time I was in a basement at a hospital. That is in the 19th to 20th in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the morning of the 20th you indicated that you were taken outside of the hospital and eventually put on buses. Did anything happen before you were placed on the buses? (3.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before we left hospital there was Major Sljivancanin there who was in command of the guards from Belgrade then. They searched us to see whether we had any valuable personal belongings and they took everything. We had to keep our hands behind our backs and head bowed, and some people were separated out from us and then they put -- they placed them aside in a group and I do not know what happened to them, but we were then placed on the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that your valuables were taken during the course of the search.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They were. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after you all were searched what happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then they put us on the buses and took us to the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there guards on the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was one and the driver of the bus. There was one soldier with an automatic rifle which he kept pointed at us so that we would not try to do anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that the buses travelled from the hospital to the Vukovar barracks. What did you see when you arrived at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that the town was completely destroyed. I saw a number of dead bodies lying around in the streets at the edge of the roadway, then we arrived at the barracks. There was an officer, a captain, who came and he would call people out as people were coming out, they were beaten so that they were all bloodied by the time they were in the yard, and then they were put on the trucks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to see what was going on outside the buses, around the barracks, other than these men being taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only saw that these people were being beaten as they were coming off the buses and there were soldiers all around, the soldiers and the volunteers and the White Eagles and they threaten us, they threaten to kill us all, that none of us has any chance of survival.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of these soldiers get on your bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They got on to the buses. They were threatening us. The ones who were sitting up front were also getting beaten. They were just hitting everybody who they could reach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the buses left the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the barracks we went to a hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where this hangar was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this was Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever been to Ovcara prior to that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the transport between the JNA barracks and Ovcara, were there still guards on the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the same guard that had been on from the hospital to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the buses arrived at Ovcara, what did you see occurring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people from the barracks were carrying with them handles of pickaxes and shovels and things like that so they had arrived before we did and they formed a gauntlet of sorts, so that -- we would get off the buses they would start beating us so that everybody was near death. They were all beaten up and broken up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point in time did you see another former JNA soldier that you knew getting off one of the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zlatko Zlogleda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you see happening to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were first soldiers in, so before me and Zlatko, Petar Kuscevic from Split, from the island of Brac came out and a Serbian soldier struck him and he said, "do not beat me, I am a JNA soldier, I was arrested by the Croatian police", so they took him aside and they asked him whether there were any other soldiers here and then he pointed at me and Zlatko Zlogleda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you were identified as a JNA soldier, what was done with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were separated out, we were placed off to the side until everybody got off the buses and taken into the hangar and locked up there and we were all taken to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any point did you enter the hangar at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. But I saw what was being done to the people in front of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is this what you have already described, the men being forced to run through the gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you left outside the hangar before you went to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About an hour and a half to two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how were you transported from Ovcara to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken in a military vehicle. There was a major there, and a soldier who was his driver, and they took us to Negoslavci. They blindfolded us and they put us in a basement of a civilian house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain at this house in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four days. About four days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the morning after this had happened, on the 21st, did you have an opportunity to speak with a JNA soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were four soldiers who guarded us. They took shifts but on -- on the morning of 20th-21st around 6 o'clock a soldier from Sabac came and said that the Chetniks slaughtered about 600 men at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the four days that you spent at Negoslavci where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to Topcider, to the barracks, that is we were taken to Belgrade, basically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what occurred after you arrived at Topcider?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They questioned us there, what we were doing, why we had fled the military. We were beaten. There were some reserve personnel and some active duty personnel, and they kept beating us for 14 days. We fainted, they did not give us anything to eat. They took us to the detention, military detention centre in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of these beatings did you sustain any injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I had a concussion and my ribs were fractured on the right-hand side and also I have some spinal injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were your ribs fractured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat us in the cinema theatre. There was a stage there and they would -- they put us up on that stage and then they would throw us down from it. That was the theatre, a hole, where they watched the movies and then they beat us with the handles of the broom sticks and things that they used to wipe and clean floors. That is what they beat us with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you accused of any crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was accused of desertion, mutiny, and theft of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there pressure put on you to sign statements admitting to these crimes, or to other crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They applied -- well, they pressured us into confessing that we killed Serbian individuals and raped and so they forced us to sign such statements where -- and these statements were what they were saying to us that happened, rather than what really happened, so we did not sign anything by our own will, just what they forced us to sign.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever taken to court on any of these charges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not taken to court for these charges, only for the armed mutiny, for the desertion and the theft of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you convicted of these charges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sentence did you receive as a result of that conviction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I received six years. I got one year off right at the sentencing so I was sentenced to five years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much of this sentence did you actually serve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that served?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Seven months in the military detention unit and seventeen in Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Valjevo a military prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, a civilian prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Valjevo is located in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you finally released from Valjevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 21st November 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that point did you return to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR.  WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time I would like to show the witness a document which we will mark as Prosecutor's exhibit...

utterances.speaker: MR.  WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: 24. Mr. Dodaj, do you remember in 1996 being interviewed by an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the course of this interview did you give a statement which was recorded in English and then translated back to you in the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was signed -- the English copy is the only one that is signed but I also had a Croatian copy, a copy in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that you gave the statement was it translated to you orally in Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me if that is your signature that appears on the copy of the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.  WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: At this time, your Honours, I would like to tender this as Prosecutor's Exhibit 24 under seal, and the Croatian version would be tendered as Prosecutor's Exhibit 24A, also under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I see there is no objection from the Defence counsel, so it is submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR.  WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila? Cross-examined by MR. FILA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for the Trial Chamber's information, there are different ways of serving sentences. There are no separate prisons where you can serve the sentences imposed by military courts. Is that correct? Can you confirm this for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how it is. We were four men from Croatia and 150 criminals there. Imagine being in such a prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree with you, but it was just a civilian prison for...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a civilian prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, there are no special military prisons. Now let us move on to the timetable. When did you move towards the JNA barracks? Approximately speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started some time between 8.30 and 10, so maybe we arrived by 11 there, at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in front of the barracks, more or less?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what time it was, about, when you arrived in Ovcara and when did you leave, because you said you stayed there for about an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We left Ovcara around -- I could not tell you precisely. I think it was about 2.30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, it was still daytime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was daylight. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
